aso-ebi: The aso ebi tells you who is family before any of them speak. After ten years of building aso ebi sets in Lagos, I have learned that the women who come to me are not looking for matching. They are looking for a version of matching that still lets them recognise themselves in the photograph. Aso ebi at its best is a quiet contract between a family and a moment: we will wear the same fabric, but we will not be the same woman.

When a bride or her sister or a friend calls me, the first question is never about the fabric. It is about the women who will wear it. How tall is the youngest one. Which of the aunties refuses sleeves. Who is pregnant. Who just had the baby. Who has not lost the weight yet and will not be lectured about it. Who is taking the wedding photographs and who is just trying to get through the day.

The fabric stays. The cuts shift. The bodice line keeps the family together while the woman keeps her own shape. The peplum forgives lunch. The sleeve sits where this particular shoulder needs it to sit. Every set in this gallery was built that way, for a sister, a friend group, a mother who refused to disappear into a room of identical outfits.
When the photographs come back two weeks later, you can see it in the order everyone stands in. The family arrives together, and each woman is still herself.
boss-ladies: These are the women who have stopped buying outfits. They are building wardrobes now. There is a difference, and you can feel it in the way they walk into a fitting. A woman buying an outfit comes in with an event. A woman building a wardrobe comes in with a calendar.

A wardrobe is what happens when the suit you wear on Monday earns the meeting that gets you the role you wear the dress to on Friday. After ten years of dressing executives in Lagos, I can tell you the wardrobe is the part of the CV most women under invest in. They will spend on the MBA, the certification, the executive coach, the leadership retreat in Cape Town. They will let the wardrobe rotate through Zara and a few inherited pieces and hope nobody notices. The wardrobe is the one part of the CV the room reads before you open your mouth.

The Boss Ladies in this gallery understood that. Each one came to me with a problem that was, on the surface, about clothes. Underneath, it was about how she wanted to be seen, remembered, and recommended. The suits, the peplum sets, the executive silhouettes in here are the answer to those questions, written in fabric.

If you are still buying outfits, the gallery will be interesting. If you are ready to build a wardrobe, this is where we start. We do not sell pieces in isolation; we build pieces that earn the next one. The colour you commission today will be the reason a board chair remembers your name six months from now.
brides: Most brides come to me with a saved photograph of someone else's wedding dress. They scroll for months, they pin twenty four pieces from twelve different houses, they walk into the atelier with a phone full of references. By the second fitting, they are wearing something none of those photos predicted. That is the work.

A wedding dress is not a costume of who you wish you were on a Tuesday. It is a careful, precise rendering of who you actually are, on the most photographed day of your life. The dresses that survive that day are the ones built around the woman, not the inspiration board. Photographs are honest. They flatten a costume into a costume. A gown built for the bride who is actually walking down the aisle carries her, even when the photograph is taken from a bad angle, even when her father holds her hand a beat too long.

So when a bride sits down with me, we put the phone away. We talk about her shoulders, where her weight sits when she is nervous, what she wants her grandmother to see in the photographs, whether the husband is the kind of man who will cry at the first look or save it for the vows. The gown that comes out the other end is the result of that conversation, not the references.

The brides in this gallery understood that. Each gown started with the woman, not the dress, and the dress came after. Some of them are still in the album of their grandmother. A few are already in storage, waiting for daughters.
soft-life: Soft Life is what comes after a woman has nothing left to prove. The pieces here are not for the boardroom, not for the wedding, not for the family aso ebi. They are for the Sunday she has earned, the brunch in Lekki she always cancels, the easy Saturday in Ikoyi that finally has nothing on the calendar, the trip she finally took to Marrakech or Cape Town or just home to the village to see her mother.

After ten years of dressing women through every promotion, every milestone, every photograph that mattered, I built this gallery for what they wear when nobody is keeping score. The fabric softens. The waist relaxes. The silhouette stops working so hard. The whole look says: I have arrived, and I am not going to spend the afternoon proving it to anyone.

The Soft Life client is rarely a first time client. She is a Boss Lady on her day off. She is a Bride three years after the wedding. She is an executive who has just stopped travelling so much. She is not new to the brand. She is the brand at its most personal, dressed for the version of her life nobody photographs for LinkedIn. The pieces are easier. The conversations at the fittings are longer. The reorders are quicker.
This is the gallery I would put a woman in if I wanted her to remember that she is allowed to be soft. The pieces here will not change her week. They will change the way she walks back into Monday.
